title: External Ventricular Drain (EVD) Management
summary: Managing an external ventricular drain for ICP monitoring and CSF drainage in neurocritical patients.
equipment: EVD system (transducer, drip chamber, collection bag)
steps: EVD is inserted by neurosurgery (bedside or OR). Nursing manages the drainage system.
LEVELING: Level the 'zero reference point' of the EVD system to the tragus of the ear (external auditory meatus) = foramen of Monro.
Set the drainage level (height above the reference) per order (commonly 10–20 cm H2O above the foramen of Monro).
Keep the drainage system closed (clamped) unless ordered for continuous or intermittent drainage.
Monitor CSF: color (clear/pink/bloody/cloudy), quantity per hour, and trend. Cloudy CSF = possible ventriculitis — notify neurosurgery.
NEVER lower the drainage chamber below the reference without an order — uncontrolled CSF drainage can cause brain herniation.
Assess EVD site dressing: intact, dry, no signs of infection. Change per policy (sterile technique).
During patient repositioning: CLAMP the EVD first, reposition, re-level, then unclamp per policy.
Monitor ICP waveform if transducer is connected: normal ICP <20 mmHg. ICP ≥20 mmHg >5 min = notify neurosurgery.
CPP (Cerebral Perfusion Pressure) = MAP − ICP. Target CPP 60–70 mmHg typically.
safetyTips: NEVER flush, irrigate, or inject anything into an EVD — can cause ventriculitis or fatal overdrainage.
Clamp before repositioning — siphon effect during movement can cause rapid overdrainage and brain herniation.
Cloudy CSF or fever = ventriculitis until proven otherwise — neurosurgery STAT notification.

title: Intracranial Pressure (ICP) Monitoring & Management
summary: Monitoring ICP values and implementing interventions to reduce elevated intracranial pressure.
equipment: Mannitol or hypertonic saline per order
steps: Normal ICP: 0–10 mmHg. Elevated ICP: ≥20 mmHg sustained >5 min requires intervention.
Position: HOB 30–45°. Head midline (avoid neck flexion or rotation which impairs venous drainage).
Avoid: coughing, suctioning without lidocaine, Valsalva, sustained hip flexion — all transiently raise ICP.
Avoid clustering care activities — space procedures to allow ICP to return to baseline.
Osmotherapy for ICP ≥20 mmHg:
Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV bolus: monitor serum osmolality (hold if >320 mOsm/L) and urine output.
Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl): monitor sodium (target 145–155 mEq/L per protocol). Via central line.
Sedation/analgesia: reduces ICP by reducing cerebral metabolic demand. Common: fentanyl + propofol or midazolam.
Avoid hypoxia (SpO2 <95%) and hypercarbia (PaCO2 >45) — both cause cerebral vasodilation and worsen ICP.
Hyperventilation (PaCO2 30–35): temporary bridge measure only (causes vasoconstriction) — use for acute herniation.
Temperature control: fever increases CMRO2 → raises ICP. Target normothermia or mild hypothermia per protocol.
safetyTips: ICP >20 mmHg sustained = notify neurosurgery. ICP >30 mmHg = brain herniation risk.
Cushing's Triad (late sign of herniation): hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations — emergency.
Never suction without pre-oxygenation and lidocaine instillation — suctioning causes a significant ICP spike.

title: Pupil Assessment (PERRLA + Grading)
summary: Assessing pupil size, shape, equality, and reactivity to monitor neurological status.
steps: Dim the room. Allow eyes to naturally dilate before assessment.
PERRLA: Pupils Equal Round Reactive to Light and Accommodation.
DIRECT RESPONSE: shine light into each eye. Observe that pupil constricts promptly (brisk) or sluggishly.
CONSENSUAL RESPONSE: when light is shone in one eye, the opposite eye should also constrict.
ACCOMMODATION: ask patient to look far away, then at your finger close up. Pupils should constrict (near response).
DOCUMENT: size in millimeters (use pupil gauge), shape (round, irregular, oval), equality (equal vs. anisocoria), and reactivity (brisk, sluggish, non-reactive, fixed).
Normal pupil: 2–6mm, equal, round, brisk reaction.
CRITICAL FINDINGS — notify provider immediately:
Fixed and dilated (blown pupil) unilaterally: CN III compression = uncal herniation.
Bilateral fixed and dilated: severe midbrain dysfunction or drug effect.
Pinpoint pupils: opioid toxicity or pontine lesion.
New anisocoria (>1mm difference): new finding always warrants notification.
safetyTips: A blown (fixed, dilated) pupil in a head-injured patient = uncal herniation — neurosurgery emergency.
Cataracts, artificial eyes, and previous eye surgery affect pupil assessment — note medical history.
Compare to baseline — a change is more significant than a single finding.
keyTakeaways: Fixed + dilated = herniation until proven otherwise

title: Lumbar Puncture (LP) Assist
summary: Assisting with lumbar puncture for CSF collection and opening pressure measurement.
equipment: LP tray (spinal needles, manometer, collection tubes 1–4, stopcock)
steps: Verify consent. Assess for contraindications: papilledema, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, local infection at site, suspected spinal cord lesion.
Obtain baseline neuro exam and vital signs.
POSITION: lateral decubent (fetal position) — chin to chest, knees to abdomen to maximize lumbar flexion. OR sitting and leaning forward over a bedside table.
Coach patient to remain very still during needle insertion. Reassure patient they will feel pressure but the area will be anesthetized.
Assist provider with sterile field setup: open LP tray, provide sterile gloves, pour prep solution.
Label CSF collection tubes 1–4 in order of collection.
After CSF collection: apply small bandage to site. Assist patient to comfortable position.
POST-LP CARE: Instruct patient to lie flat for 1–4 hours per protocol (reduces post-LP headache risk).
Monitor for post-LP headache (worst when upright, relieved supine): encourage oral fluids, caffeine, acetaminophen. Severe/persistent headache = blood patch may be needed.
Transport labeled tubes to lab immediately (CSF glucose degrades quickly).
safetyTips: Do NOT perform LP with suspected increased ICP without CT head first — risk of herniation if mass lesion present.
If patient moves during needle placement, provider must stop. Coach stillness carefully.
Bloody tap: tubes 1 and 4 — if tube 4 clears, suggests traumatic tap. True SAH: xanthochromia and equal blood all tubes.
keyTakeaways: CT head before LP if papilledema or focal neuro deficits
